result:
There's something quietly fascinating about the way we build cities. We take raw land — forests, meadows, riverbanks — and we pour concrete over it in an act of relentless ambition. Then, almost immediately, we spend the rest of our lives trying to get back to what we buried. We plant gardens in window boxes. We go on vacations to the wilderness we once destroyed. We pay thousands of dollars for "wellness retreats" in the woods.

I think this tension lives in all of us. We want progress and we want peace. We chase innovation but crave nostalgia. We build faster phones but complain that the world moves too fast.

And yet, there's something beautiful about the contradiction. It means we're always reaching, always dissatisfied, always hoping that the next place we arrive will finally feel like home. Maybe that dissatisfaction isn't a flaw. Maybe it's the engine behind every song ever written, every painting, every late-night conversation that stretched past midnight because neither person wanted to say goodbye.

The truth is, we are creatures caught between the wild and the ordered, the ancient and the modern. We carry stone tools in our lizard brains and quantum computers in our hands. And somehow, against all odds, we keep showing up for each other — sharing meals, telling stories, building fragile little communities on top of concrete.

Maybe the city is just another campfire. Maybe it always was.
